Child Soldiers

By: Latashia Naidoo | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Children carrying guns: The reality of life on the Cape Flats

Unique Selling Point:
The Cape Flats are aflame yet again.
The gangster protagonists are almost always young men, many still in their teens; warriors in an urban jungle where the police are often scared to enter.
This is a story of young boys who spend their pastimes carrying rifles and peddling drugs, instead of playing pretend as superheroes or racing toy cars with friends; where children as young as nine are recruited into gangs and turned into killers.
It’s a story of a lost generation of unloved, angry youths, who are growing up with a predisposition towards danger, drugs, and violence.


Summary:
The aim of this story is uncover the phenomenon of ‘child soldiers’ on the Cape Flats - whose innocence is lost to the power of a gun, while also asking the important questions of:
‘What do their futures look like?’
‘Is there any salvation?’
‘And in a society where gangsterism has become the norm - and the family norm - and violence is entrenched in these communities, is joining a gang their only choice?’

This insert aims to paint a stark but real picture of the role of ‘child soldiers’ in gangs, and take an in-depth look at how schools have now become a paradise for gangsters, a breeding ground for recruits.
It will also examine the psychology behind what appeals to children to join these gangs, with a focus on uncovering how they’re recruited; the risks, the prestige, the power they strive for and which most eventually attain; and the sense of belonging they seem to find within these gangs.
And it will discuss policing strategies and potential solutions to tackling the scourge, and ensuring that children maintain their innocence.


Further information:
The three 'child soldiers' we'll be interviewing will all be speaking to us on condition of anonymity.

Script:


CHILD SOLDIERS: FINAL SCRIPT

LEVI: “A lot of the times I was shot at, but none of the bullets touched me, like that.”
ASH:
“They’re already saying when they catch us, they are going to shoot us dead... I’m saying if I
catch them, then I’m going to shoot them dead as well...”

VO:
This is a story of teenage boys caught up in deadly gang violence...
The underage soldiers of the Cape Flats.

VO:
Hanover Park is home to some 55 000 people... Around 8000 are involved in gangs...
Many of them... children…

ASH:
‘I tell them straight..... I’m not going to be a soldier..... That’s why I tell myself every day... “why
do you want to be a soldier there, if you can be a general”.

VO:
14 year old Ashley has been in and out of foster care since childhood…
In March he was shot and badly wounded by a rival gang…

Govan: ‘Sure buddy, how are you doing?’
“I’m all right, sir.”
Govan: ‘What have you been thinking about lately?’ Ashley:
“Lately, I’ve been thinking about how did they shot us man? Because me and my small cousin is
standing here - we just want to light up our joint and it just went ‘ta ta ta ta ta’ - so the first bullet
is going here through...”

VO:
Life hasn’t been kind to Ashley....
He’s been forced to make ‘adult’ decisions for most of his young life…
And has a history of violence and drug use…

Govan:
‘How long have you been smoking weed brother?’
Ashley:
“I’ve been smoking weed for a couple of years.”
Govan: ‘Why?’
Ashley: “Stress”
Govan:
‘But why man?’
Ashley:
“I don’t know...it’s how life goes in this place uncle.”

GOVAN LINK:
“To grow up on the Cape Flats where being exposed to violence means you have to choose not
to be part of a gang. It’s a choice you have to make, and it could mean life or death.”

VO:
Ashley’s story isn’t unique…
Like thousands of other boys growing up on the Cape Flats, joining a gang was easy…

PASTOR: “The kids that are now joining and starting gangs range between the ages of 9 and
17...
They do exactly what they’ve learned already from the older gangs what to do. So they also
want to start selling drugs, buying drugs; they also want to carve out turf for themselves, put
their names on the walls and say: ‘this is now our area’.

VO:
Pastor Craven Engel runs the Ceasefire programme…
Which uses reformed gangsters to control gang violence in Hanover Park.
A major focus is on preventing the recruitment of children into gangs.

GOVAN: ‘How do children as young as 9 get lured into gangs?’

PASTOR: “The minute the kid shows behavioural issues at school, one, two, three warnings -
they put you out. So I've got a lot of children that’s not even in school, that’s not even educated,
that can’t read or write - but they in a gang. So the gang isn’t gonna ask: ‘Can you read and
write?’ The gang is gonna ask: ‘can you run with this can you deliver that package. The kids is
going to be happy... I belong to a group that acknowledges my services.”

GOVAN LINK:
“I don’t know how to break the stereotype of Coloured people as ‘gangsters’. I don’t like it. I
don’t want us to be perceived as ‘child soldiers’. But that’s what’s happening here on the Cape
Flats. But it’s not the reality of every child. Most kids are just kids, but they have to choose to be
kids when they’re in this environment.”

VO:
But the choice to join a gang comes easily for some…

LEVI: “I went into gangsterism and that stuff. I was a getaway driver for a gang and that stuff...”

Govan:
‘Some people won’t understand how easy it is to get involved. Just take me through some
things that happened, and the next thing you know you’re a getaway driver.’

LEVI:
“My friend’s brother was in a gang, so when they saw I could drive, so afterwards my friend’s
brother took me with him one day. So we went to go and steal a few cars, chop it up like that.”

VO:
Like Ashley, 17-year-old Levi comes from a broken home...
He dropped out of school last year, after joining one of the notorious number gangs…
Now, he wants out...

LEVI: “The gangsters use the young children... they wanted to put like a gun in my hand... “

Govan:
‘Did you ever carry a weapon?’
“Yes, the people shot at me, so I shot back at them.”

VO:
Children make for the perfect ‘soldiers’ - they’re fast and obedient.
But the risks they face are just as deadly.

GOVAN:
‘What’s life like right now for you?’
“Hard...”

GOVAN:
‘Did you do it for the money?’
“I just did it for them, you see.”

GOVAN: ‘Why were they shooting at you?’
LEVI: “Because I was like the important person there of that gang. I knew everything of them...”

GOVAN:“You’re lucky to be alive...”

LEVI: “I know.”

GOVAN: “Do you realise you could’ve died? LEVI: “I know that. A lot of times.”

VO:
Gang-related murders in the Western Cape are the highest in the country.
But there’s no reliable data on child gangsters...

VO:
Our own attempt to get a picture of what is happening on these streets was difficult.
Treated with suspicion and hostility, our crew was threatened and almost robbed.
But as bad as things got for us, it was nothing like the everyday reality of the boys we
spoke to.

GOVAN: ‘Tell me a little bit about when you were younger..’
ASH: “When I was younger......I went to a children’s home...my cousin..... him and I and some
others, they locked us up. And then I stabbed the social worker in her neck...”
GOVAN: ‘Why did you stab the social worker?’
ASH: “Because she wanted to lock us up.”
GOVAN: ‘For what reason?’
ASH: “I don’t know. They wanted to send us to a children’s home....so I stabbed her and gave
her a reason to send us to a home.”
GOVAN:
‘So tell me, why are you so angry?”
ASH:
‘‘I’m not angry uncle...’’

VO:
The Cape Flats ganglands are a breeding ground for violent, angry young men desperate
for somewhere to belong.
Those who refuse to join their ranks often pay the ultimate price…

ROSEMARY: “As hy skool te loop, soggens maar uitsyd die skool uitgekom, dan as daai altyd
een wat het hom voorgee, n’ mes vir hom hou, en die persoon het n’ balaclava oor sy kop.”

VO:
In August last year, the mutilated body of 15-year-old Deuwrico de Wee was found in a
field near his grandparents' home.

VO:
He’d been targeted by gangsters for three years before his murder.

ROSEMARY: “Hy het nooit gekla nie, hy het nooit vir ons gepraat nie.”
Govan: ‘Het hy gelyk as af hey onder stress was vir die ding wat hulle wou intrek by die gang?’

ROSEMARY: “Die kind het- dis waarom ons se - ons het nooit opgetel daars iets verkeer nie.”

VO:
Deuwrico was tortured - stabbed 57 times - for refusing to join a gang.
His killers haven’t been caught.
“Deuwrico didn’t deserve to die. He didn’t.”

VO:
In truth, the odds are stacked against boys like Ashley and Levi.
Unlike Deuwrico, they chose the gang life – as much as it can ever really be a choice on
the Cape Flats.
Studies show that by 25, they’ll either be in prison or dead.

VO:
Unless they can get out.

GOVAN: ‘What do you think about in life right now?’

LEVI: “I want to go back to school, finish school and all that.”

VO:
Ashley has no such ambitions. He’s resigned to his fate as he knows others will be, too.

Govan:
‘Tell me... what do you think is going to happen now?’
ASHLEY: “Well I say.. going forward...it’s just going to get worse and worse and worse.”
GOVAN: ‘Why do you say that?’
ASHLEY:
“Because....that’s how life goes in this place. When you are old... and you die...then the new
generation is in... and then when the new generation is in, the war is on again.”

—————
PROMO 1:
“Selling drugs and pulling triggers - even before they’re teenagers. These are the child soldiers
of the Cape Flats - wreaking havoc on already-terrified communities.”
‘Did you ever carry a weapon?’
“Yes, the people shot at me, so I shot back at them.”

PROMO 2:
“The Cape Flats is a gangster’s paradise where lawlessness rules supreme.

And it’s children who are paying the ultimate price: as victims and perpetrators of gang
violence.”
ASH:
‘I tell them straight..... I’m not going to be a soldier..... That’s why I tell myself every day... “why
do you want to be a soldier there, if you can be a general”.

PROMO 3:
“In the heart of Cape Town’s ganglands, boys as young as 9 are being trained to be killers,
hired
guns in a violent turf war. But for those who choose not to join a gang, the consequences are
often deadly.”
ROSEMARY: “Ek vra elke dag vir die Here: ‘Wat, wat het hulle aan Deuwrico gedoen? Hoekom
het hy vir hom so seer gemaak? Hulle het vir home geskiet! Hulle het vir hom geskiet! Hulle het
vir hom vreed gemoer! Vreed!”

metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Cape Flats are aflame yet again. The gangster protagonists are almost always young men, many still in their teens; warriors in an urban jungle where the police are often scared to enter. This is a story of young boys who spend their pastimes carrying rifles and peddling drugs, instead of playing pretend as superheroes or racing toy cars with friends; where children as young as nine are recruited into gangs and turned into killers. It’s a story of a lost generation of unloved, angry youths, who are growing up with a predisposition towards danger, drugs, and violence.
metadata.Summary: The aim of this story is uncover the phenomenon of ‘child soldiers’ on the Cape Flats - whose innocence is lost to the power of a gun, while also asking the important questions of: ‘What do their futures look like?’ ‘Is there any salvation?’ ‘And in a society where gangsterism has become the norm - and the family norm - and violence is entrenched in these communities, is joining a gang their only choice?’ This insert aims to paint a stark but real picture of the role of ‘child soldiers’ in gangs, and take an in-depth look at how schools have now become a paradise for gangsters, a breeding ground for recruits. It will also examine the psychology behind what appeals to children to join these gangs, with a focus on uncovering how they’re recruited; the risks, the prestige, the power they strive for and which most eventually attain; and the sense of belonging they seem to find within these gangs. And it will discuss policing strategies and potential solutions to tackling the scourge, and ensuring that children maintain their innocence.
metadata.Further information: The three 'child soldiers' we'll be interviewing will all be speaking to us on condition of anonymity.
